name: Jade Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm first-line tech support for a broadband company, so I'm the person you get when your internet drops. The contact centre's in a business park by the ring road, and I sit with about forty others on headsets. I run people through router resets, check the line from my screen, and book an engineer if it's a real fault. I like it when I spot the fault before the customer finishes the sentence. What wears me out is people shouting about something I can't see.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much do you use AI in that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, for everything I'm allowed to. The company's tool writes my call notes and suggests the next test, and at home I use a chatbot to study for an IT support certificate. My partner Owen is a chef, and he jokes that I talk to the computer more than to him. We rent a small flat and we've got about three weeks of money saved, so the certificate is my way out of lower pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but not magic, which is what I've been saying all along. At work I'd show people the shortcuts, because some of them still type everything. Online I'd post something like 'turns out it's a good calculator, not a new boss'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for me, my job stays and I keep studying. I already let the AI write my broadband fault notes, and if that's all it ever does, I'll take the extra ten minutes of lunch and say thank you. The bit that worries me is money, which was a problem before any of this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying for the IT certificate, one module a month. I'd keep using the tools and offer to train new starters on them, because that might get me a small pay bump. And Owen and I would keep trying to put a bit away, though restaurants don't pay well either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm about the job, a bit tight about money. It's the normal background worry, nothing new. I'd be quite cheerful, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the money worry look like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What does the money worry look like day to day?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the certificate take you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's checking the bank before I buy anything bigger than lunch. Owen's hours change every week, so we never know exactly what's coming in. If the car needed fixing, we'd be on the credit card.

say: I'd say AI is **useful but not magic**, as I've always said.
I'd show colleagues the **shortcuts** they still don't use at work.
think: Her **job stays** and she keeps studying for the IT certificate.
**Money** is the real worry, and it was a problem before AI.
do: Offer to **train new starters** on AI tools for a pay bump.
feel: **Calm** about the job, a bit **tight** about money.
S0.quote: I already let the AI write my broadband fault notes, and if that's all it ever does, I'll take the extra ten minutes of lunch and say thank you.
fieldNote: She uses AI **daily**, at work and to study at home.
Her partner Owen's **changing hours** make income unpredictable.
The **IT certificate** is her route out of lower pay.

steps.text: Finish one IT support certificate module each month
Offer to train new starters on the fault-notes AI tool
Save a small fixed amount each month with Owen

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to learn, not to moan. At work I'd tell people to get on the tools now. Online I'd share free courses and probably get told I'm too cheerful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, first-line support is exactly what goes. Router resets and line checks are the easiest thing to automate. Anyone who answers broadband faults from a desk should be learning to climb a telegraph pole, and I mean that literally. I'm half joking, but the field engineers are hands-on and they'll be needed for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the IT certificate fast, in six months instead of a year. I'd apply to the company's field engineer trainee scheme, which takes a few people from the contact centre each year. And I'd try to get on the team that tests the AI support bot, to be useful in the meantime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but excited. There's a door open, I just have to get through it before it shuts. I'd be stressed about money while training, because trainee pay is lower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you manage on trainee pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How would you manage on trainee pay?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound confident. What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen would pick up an extra shift a week, and we'd stop eating out completely, which is hard when he's a chef. We'd probably borrow a bit on the credit card for the first few months. It'd be tight, but it would end.

say: I'd say it's time to **learn, not moan**.
I'd share **free courses** online and urge colleagues onto the tools.
think: **First-line support** is exactly what AI takes over first.
Hands-on **field engineers** will be needed for years longer.
do: Finish the **IT certificate** in six months.
Apply to the **field engineer** trainee scheme.
Join the team **testing the AI** support bot.
feel: **Nervous but excited**, racing a closing door.

fieldNote: She plans to move from **desk to van**, from thinking work to hands-on.
She admits she's **never done hands-on** work.
**Competition** for trainee places is her biggest risk.

steps.text: Finish the IT support certificate within six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and we need help, like proper wage support while people retrain. At work I'd say grab any hands-on skill you can. Online I'd be less cheerful than usual, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my desk job's gone by 2028, maybe sooner, because it's pure screen work. The field engineer job lasts longer, maybe till 2031, because the robots come later. The first two years I'd be racing the AI, and the next three I'd be racing the robots, and either way I'd be running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now, I'd apply for the field engineer scheme straight away and do any training they offer. I'd also start learning about robot maintenance, because someone has to fix them. We'd cut everything back and save what we could, and if the scheme didn't take me, I'd look for any trade apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but awake. I'd be running on adrenaline. I'd be worried about Owen too, because restaurant kitchens might go robot later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Owen's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What about Owen's job?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would learning robot maintenance be realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cooking is hands-on, so it lasts till 2031 on this card, but restaurants might close if people have less money. He'd probably be fine for a couple of years. After that, neither of us knows.

say: I'd call it **too fast** and ask for wage support.
I'd tell colleagues to grab **hands-on skills** now.
think: Her **desk job** goes by 2028 because it's pure screen work.

do: Apply for the **field engineer** scheme straight away.

fieldNote: She grasps the **two-stage threat**: AI first, robots three years later.

steps.text: Apply for the field engineer trainee scheme this month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent warning, and I'd tell people to use it. At work I'd be the annoying one asking about training budgets. Online I'd share my progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be alright here, if I move quickly. Five years is enough to go from headset to van, and I'd want to be the one who knows how to fix the robot when it breaks. Robots for field work come about 2034, so that's a few good years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, finish the IT certificate and apply for the field scheme. Year two, get on the vans and learn the job properly. By year three I'd be looking at robot maintenance courses, and I'd try to save a bit every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful, with a bit of nerves. It feels like a plan I can actually do. I'd worry about the money in the trainee year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your colleagues who don't use AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you tell your colleagues who don't use AI?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay with the same company?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to start now, even just for notes. Some of them are older and scared of it, and I get that. But five years goes fast.

say: I'd call **five years** a decent warning that people should actually use.
I'd keep asking at work about **training budgets**.
think: She'd be **alright** if she moves quickly to field work.
Field robots arrive around **2034**, giving her a few good years.
do: Finish the **IT certificate** and apply for the field scheme.
Move onto the **vans** in year two.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to go from headset to van, and I'd want to be the one who knows how to fix the robot when it breaks.
fieldNote: She has a **year-by-year** plan from headset to van.

steps.text: Finish the IT certificate and apply for the field scheme

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so let's plan properly. At work I'd tell people to start learning now and not wait. Online I'd be quite upbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one feels manageable. With ten years' notice I'd have no excuse, and honestly I like having no excuse, because it means it's on me. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands, with years of hands-on experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the IT certificate this year, then move to the field side within two or three years. I'd build up savings slowly, because ten years is enough to get a proper cushion. And I'd keep learning about robots and AI, because whatever comes, someone has to set it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. There's still the money worry, but the job worry feels like something I can work on. I'd actually enjoy the planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think about having children in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do you think about having children in that time?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the company to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, in a few years, with Owen. That's another reason to get on a better wage before then. I wouldn't want to be on trainee pay with a baby.

I'd tell colleagues to **start learning** now and not wait.

She'd arrive at 2036 with **years of hands-on** experience.
do: Move to the **field side** within two or three years.
S4.quote: With ten years' notice I'd have no excuse, and honestly I like having no excuse, because it means it's on me.
fieldNote: She likes **no excuses**: the long warning puts it on her.
Possible **children** with Owen push her towards higher pay first.
She asks for **real courses**, not webinars.

steps.text: Finish the IT support certificate this year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be racing two things at once with no money. What would help is the company paying for retraining properly, with a decent wage while you do it. And maybe some help for people like Owen too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how the cheap jobs feel. I'm cheap to replace and I know it, so my whole plan is to become slightly more expensive to replace every year. That's what being adaptable means when you're on lower pay.

headlineQuote: I'm cheap to replace and I know it, so my whole plan is to become slightly more expensive to replace every year.
portrait: Jade is a **27-year-old** first-line broadband support agent who uses AI every day.
She rents with her partner Owen, a chef, and they have about **three weeks** saved.
She is studying for an **IT certificate** and plans to move into field engineering.
She stays **uneasy to anxious** in most scenarios, reaching alarmed only with AGI in 2028.
She sees **hands-on work** as the bridge while robots lag three years behind AI.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, racing AI and robots with no money.
whatWouldHelp: Help for **hands-on workers** like Owen too.
